stem: A client using an insulin pump develops an unexplained rapid glucose rise. Which safety principle is most important?

options.A: Observe the glucose rise for several hours before checking the infusion system because brief pump interruptions rarely lead to ketosis.
options.B: Infusion-set dislodgement or occlusion can interrupt insulin delivery and increase the risk of ketosis or DKA, so pump problems must be recognized and managed early.
options.C: Once pump settings are stable, infusion-set problems are unlikely to alter glucose rapidly because the body maintains a large depot of long-acting insulin.
options.D: Pump users can reduce glucose monitoring after the first week because device malfunction is usually detected before meaningful hyperglycemia or ketosis develops.

rationale: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 state that insulin-infusion complications from infusion-set dislodgement or occlusion place pump users at risk for ketosis and DKA and must be recognized and managed early. Safe pump use also requires understanding how to troubleshoot the system. B directly reflects this guidance. A delays recognition, C incorrectly assumes a protective long-acting insulin depot, and D conflicts with the need to detect interruption-related hyperglycemia promptly.
educational_objective: Recognize unexplained rapid hyperglycemia in an insulin-pump user as a possible infusion-set interruption and troubleshoot promptly because dislodgement or occlusion can lead to ketosis and DKA.
source_organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes
source_document_title: 7. Diabetes Technology: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
source_locator: Section 'Complications and Challenges of Infusing Insulin'; general device principles/troubleshooting discussion.
source_claim_supported: Infusion-set dislodgement and occlusion can interrupt infused insulin and place users at risk for ketosis and DKA; these problems must be recognized and managed early, and users need troubleshooting knowledge.

source_original.stem: A client using an insulin pump develops an unexplained rapid glucose rise. Which safety principle is most important?

options.A: An unexplained glucose rise can be observed for several hours before checking the infusion set, because brief pump interruptions rarely cause ketosis.
options.B: Infusion-set dislodgement or occlusion can interrupt rapid-acting insulin delivery and lead to ketosis or DKA, so pump problems must be recognized and managed early.
options.C: Once pump settings are stable, infusion-set problems are unlikely to alter glucose rapidly because the body maintains a large depot of long-acting insulin.
options.D: Pump users can reduce glucose monitoring after the first week of therapy because device malfunction is usually detected before meaningful hyperglycemia or ketosis develops.

source_original.rationale: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 state that infusion-set dislodgement and occlusion place pump users at risk for ketosis and DKA and must be recognized and managed early; pump education includes troubleshooting. Option B reflects that risk. Option A delays troubleshooting. Option C incorrectly assumes a protective long-acting insulin depot. Option D inappropriately reduces monitoring despite the possibility of device interruption.
source_original.source_detail: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 7 Diabetes Technology — Complications and Challenges of Infusing Insulin: infusion-set dislodgement and occlusion can interrupt insulin delivery, creating risk for ketosis/DKA, and must be recognized and managed early; pump education includes troubleshooting. FDA 2026 insulin-pump recall data independently corroborate that insulin under-delivery can cause severe hyperglycemia and DKA. Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Diabetes Care 49(Suppl 1), published 2025-12-08 for 2026; current annual ADA guideline and FDA 2026 device safety data rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: medication administration, calculations, adverse effects/interactions, monitoring and client teaching. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained construct and key. Removed the unnecessary statement that the pump necessarily delivers rapid-acting insulin from the keyed option so the final claim exactly matches the ADA infusion-set interruption guidance without adding formulation-specific precision.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Insulin-pump infusion-set failure and DKA risk
audit_findings.source_authority: Current ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026.

audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item uses only the guideline's explicit dislodgement/occlusion, ketosis/DKA and early-recognition claims.

distractor_audit.A: Dangerously delays troubleshooting and contradicts early recognition.
distractor_audit.C: Invents a long-acting insulin depot that defeats the pump-interruption construct.
distractor_audit.D: Unsupported reduction in monitoring and contradicts need for early detection.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B matches the current guideline.
audit_findings.cueing: No numeric cue or second plausible safety principle.
